newsitem.title: RUSSIA: CIS leaders to consider security on Afghan border.
newsitem.headline: CIS leaders to consider security on Afghan border.

text.p: Leaders of Russia and four former central Asian republics were due to meet on Friday to discuss extra security in southern border areas following the rise to power in Afghanistan of the hardline Islamic Taleban militia.

The summit of the five Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) countries in the Kazakh capital Almaty reflects concern in the Kremlin that the Taleban's drive to extend their control over Afghanistan could destabilise the former Soviet republics of Central Asia.

President Boris Yeltsin, preparing for heart surgery later this year, called for the meeting earlier this week. His security chief Alexander Lebed warned that failure to act could have serious implications for Russian national security.

Moscow regards the southern flank of the CIS, a loose grouping erected on the ashes of the former Soviet Union, as its strategic underbelly and Russian border guards patrol Tajikistan's 1,500-km (900-mile) frontier with Afghanistan.
The Afghan border has become an effective front line in a prolonged conflict between the pro-Moscow Tajik government in Dushanbe and Islamic guerrillas based in Afghanistan.
"We are following developments closely," General Andrei Nikolayev, head of the Russian border guards, told Russian Public Television.

The Almaty summit was expected to be attended by the presidents of four of the 12 CIS states -- Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan. Russia was due to be represented by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
"I think a proposal will be worked out at this meeting that will ensure our common security in the region," Nikolayev said.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov told NTV television on Wednesday that Moscow wanted a common position over Afghanistan with the Central Asian states and added that the danger of destabilisation was "not exaggerated".

Afghanistan's Taleban fighters seized the capital Kabul and have advanced north towards areas controlled by a powerful warlord, General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who holds sway over areas bordering former Soviet republics.
The outspoken Lebed, secretary of Russia's policy-making Security Council, said on Tuesday that the triumph of the Taleban was fraught with danger for Moscow and its CIS partners.

Lebed, a veteran of the Soviet Afghan war whose harsh statements on foreign policy have caused the Kremlin headaches in the past, said Russia should render all necessary help to the Afghan government driven out of Kabul last week.

But most top Moscow officials, still haunted by the memory of their ill-fated intervention in Afghanistan from 1979 to 1989, appeared extremely cautious about any suggestion of helping any of the parties in the conflict.

Primakov, asked about Lebed's comments, said: "We are a long way from sympathising with the Taleban movement, that's clear. But I think we should wait... Only after this summit...will we take a decision. I don't think we should act alone."
Lebed said the Taleban wanted to take control of parts of Uzbekistan, including the ancient Islamic centre of Bukhara.
Uzbekistan, which maintains contacts with Uzbeks living in northern Afghanistan and controlled by the ethnic Uzbek Dostum, has kept silent on the Taleban offensive.
Kazakhstan has expressed concern about developments in Afghanistan and called for a U.N. Security Council meeting on the issue.
